claims.text: High interface density is the primary cause of enhanced resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings.
The proposed coatings consist of alternating layers having distinct compositions and microstructures.
Reducing layer thickness increases interface density.
A homogeneous HEA coating with the same overall composition provides a baseline without engineered multilayer interfaces.
At approximately 1000 K, diffusion and dislocation climb will be active under suitable creep stresses.
Restriction of atomic diffusion by interfaces increases the effective activation energy for creep.
Blocking dislocation motion and suppressing diffusion reduce the steady-state creep strain rate relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
Multilayer coatings with thinner layers and higher interface densities will have lower creep strain rates than homogeneous coatings.
Dislocations will accumulate at multilayer interfaces after creep testing.
The proposed interface mechanism will predominate at elevated temperatures and moderate-to-high stresses where diffusion and dislocation motion are thermally activated.
The influence of interfaces may diminish at lower temperatures.
At extreme stresses, phase transformation or dynamic recrystallization may supersede the proposed interface-controlled mechanism.
The relative contributions of diffusion suppression and dislocation blocking are not yet determined.
Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate reduction relative to the homogeneous control would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe dislocation pile-ups at interfaces would by itself falsify the overall interface-barrier hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism posits two pathways—dislocation blocking and diffusion suppression—but the falsification rule treats absence of dislocation pile-ups alone as sufficient to falsify the overall hypothesis, even if diffusion suppression and a lower creep rate are observed.
